title: Projects

content:
The features were finished last week. This week was about getting Atlas out of my laptop, documenting it, and making sure I can explain every part of it.
What I worked on # Deployment. Atlas now runs on a server. GitHub Actions builds and tests the project and pushes a Docker image to Docker Hub. On the server, Docker Compose runs the database, Atlas, Caddy for HTTPS and Watchtower, which pulls a new image when there is one. Documentation. I updated the README with the most important user stories and the deployment setup. The user stories and a class diagram now live in their own files, and the README links to them. Exam preparation. I wrote an outline for the presentation, went through user story 4 (creating a mention) from the first request to the database, and tested myself with questions until I could explain the difficult parts in my own words. Reflections # Deployment and configuration problems Almost nothing I fixed was a bug in the code. A secret had the wrong name, the compiler did not find Lombok on the newest Java version, and an old version of Docker Compose could not recreate a container. Each time the answer was in a log, so I learned to read the log before guessing.
Reflecting. Mentions have no foreign keys, so the service has to check that the pages exist. Notifications are saved before they are sent, so a message can arrive twice but never get lost. Every design choice in Atlas had a cost, and knowing the cost is what makes it a choice and not a guess.
Challenges # Keeping the documentation true. The project changed a lot, so diagrams and texts from the early weeks no longer matched. I had to go through them and decide what to update and what to keep as a record of how the project grew.
What is next # The exam. After that I want to clean up the exception handling, split the configuration class and add the things I left out on purpose, such as search, pagination and a frontend.
title: Week 10 — Wrap Up

content:
In week 5 I wrote down where Atlas might need concurrency. This week I built it, and each part solves one of those problems.
What I worked on # Devlogs as a changelog. Admins write them and everyone reads them. Creating a devlog sends a notification to every user from a thread pool, so the admin gets an answer at once. A job for time capsules. One scheduled thread checks every minute for capsules that have opened, and sends one notification for each. A WebSocket. A ConnectionRegistry keeps track of the open connections, and new notifications are pushed to the user the moment they are created. Tests for the rate limiter, the job and the WebSocket. Reflections # Concurrency problems live in shared state. My rate limiter from last week keeps a list of timestamps per user. A thread-safe map is not enough, because “count the requests” and “add this one” are two steps. Two threads can both see 9 of 10 and both get in. A lock around both steps fixes it. The same thinking applies to the WebSocket connections: Jetty does not allow two threads to write to the same connection at once.
Timecapsule notifications. For time capsules I save the notification first and mark the capsule as notified afterwards. If the server stops in between, the worst case is a duplicate. The other order could lose a message, which seemed worse.
WebSockets skip my security filter. The filter only covers HTTP routes, so the token has to be checked when the connection opens. Browsers cannot set an Authorization header on a WebSocket, so the token goes in the URL. That works, but it can end up in logs. In a bigger project I would send it as the first message instead.
Green tests can hide errors. After the WebSocket tests passed, I saw a database error in the log. A background thread was still writing notifications when the next test cleared the database. The fix was to make the test wait for the background work to finish. It taught me to read the log even when the tests are green.
Challenges # The WebSocket closed after about 30 seconds because it was idle. The server now pings every 20 seconds, which keeps it open.
Next week # I will focus on understanding the project and preparing for the exam. After that, I want to clean up the exception handling and split the configuration class, which has taken on too many jobs.
title: Week 9 — Concurrency & WebSockets

content:
After testing the API in week 7, I spent this week making it safer and tidier. I wanted to look at Atlas the way someone who did not build it would.
What I worked on # Roles. Role now implements Javalin’s RouteRole, so an admin-only route is marked on the route itself and checked in one place. The token only holds the user id, and I read the role from the database on every request. An AI rate limit. Each user can ask Gemini for 10 prompts per hour, and the answer length is capped, so one user cannot run up the bill. Long text. Content columns are now TEXT, because a normal string column stops at 255 characters, which is too short for a memory. Time capsules. I removed the stored isLocked field and calculate the lock status from the unlock date instead. Titles. I removed the rule that page titles must be unique. Reflections # Endpoint roles. Putting Role.ADMIN on the route means the rule is visible next to the endpoint, and nobody has to remember to add a check in a controller. I think this is much harder to forget than an if statement inside each method.
JWT role not stored in token. If it were, a user who loses admin rights would keep them until the token expires. Reading it from the database costs one extra query per request, but a role change takes effect at once. For this project, that trade-off is worth it.
Timecapsules locked state. A stored isLocked flag can disagree with the unlock date, for example when nobody updates it. Calculating it from the date means it can never be wrong.
A decision I changed. I first made titles unique to avoid confusion when linking pages. But links use ids, so duplicates are not a technical problem. The confusion is about how a list looks, and the frontend can solve that by showing the page type and subtitle. Removing the check also removed the same code from nine services, which made the project simpler.
Challenges # Nobody can make themselves an admin through the API, on purpose, so I promote my own user directly in the database. Locally the database is also recreated on every start, so I have to do it again each time.
Next week # Concurrency in practice: a scheduled job for time capsules, a thread pool for notifications, and a WebSocket to push them live.
title: Week 8 — Security & Hardening

content:
This week was about testing the API end to end, and the tests found more than I expected.
What I worked on # REST Assured tests for every controller. Each test class starts the real Javalin server and sends real HTTP requests to a PostgreSQL database in a Testcontainers Docker container. A TestPopulator seeds the data and a cleanup method resets it between tests. Gherkin. I wrote a feature file with scenarios in the form Given a valid token, when I send POST /chapters, then I get 201. Notifications and devlogs, built as a complete flow with tests. Mentions and ownership. I connected each mention to its user and added checks so users cannot read other users’ mentions. Configuration. I moved the JWT secret into config.properties, and made the database reset on start only when the app is not deployed. Reflections # Tests as a design tool. While writing the mention tests I asked what happens if I link to a page that belongs to someone else. The answer was that it worked, which meant a user could attach links to other people’s pages. That is a security hole, not a small bug. The fix was to check in the service that both pages exist and belong to the logged-in user.
404 instead of 403. When a user asks for another user’s page, I answer 404 Not Found. A 403 Forbidden would confirm that the page exists. Hiding that is a small privacy gain for no extra code.
Gherkin versus REST Assured. Gherkin describes behaviour in plain language, and REST Assured checks it in code. I did not set up Cucumber, so my feature file is a specification, and each scenario matches one REST Assured test. For a project this size that was enough, and it kept the tests close to what the API promises.
A secret in the source code. I had written the JWT secret directly in the code, and I noticed it only when I looked at the project the way someone else would. Secrets belong in configuration that is not committed.
Challenges # All the endpoint tests share one database and one port, so they have to clean up after themselves, or a failing test can break the next one. Getting the setup and cleanup right took more time than writing the tests.
Next week # Roles and admin-only routes, and hardening what the tests showed me.
title: Week 7 — Rest assured

content:
This was the most productive week so far. The API went from one working resource to almost all of them.
What I worked on # JWT. A generator and a verifier, so every request except login and registration needs a token. EndpointGroup. Each controller registers its own routes, instead of main knowing every path. A full flow for chapters: DTOs, mapper, service and controller, tested with HTTP files. AbstractController. One generic controller with create, get by id, list, update, delete and random. After chapters, memories, stories, artifacts, people, places, fragments, time capsules and lists each needed little more than DTOs, a mapper, a service and a small subclass. Dependency injection in ApplicationConfig, which grew with every resource. Reflections # The signal to abstract. I only wrote the generic controller after I had written the chapter flow by hand and could see which parts repeated. Doing it earlier would have been guessing. The result is that adding a new resource is now fast and consistent.
An abstraction has a cost. Not everything fits. Authentication, users and mentions do different things, so they do not extend AbstractController. I decided it is better to let a few controllers stand alone than to bend the base class until it fits everything.
The user id comes from the token, never from the request. A client should not be able to say “I am user 5”. The token proves who they are, and the service uses that id for every query. That decision is what makes it possible to keep every user’s data private.
Small bugs showed the value of interfaces. The mappers for people and places had a mistake that I found only because I made them implement a shared IMapper interface. The interface forced the same signature everywhere.
Challenges # ApplicationConfig is getting long. Every new resource needs its own block of DAO, mapper, service and controller. It works and it is easy to follow, but I can see it becoming hard to read if it keeps growing.
Next week # Test every endpoint properly with REST Assured instead of clicking through HTTP files, and describe the behaviour in Gherkin.
title: Week 6 — Rest API

content:
This week’s topic was concurrency. Instead of adding threads to the project just to say I had used them, I wanted to find out where Atlas really needs them.
What I worked on # Logging. I added SLF4J and Logback and replaced my print statements with proper log messages. The first complete flow. For the user, JSON now arrives in the controller, gets validated in the service and is saved by the DAOs. Authentication controller. I split login and registration out of the user controller into a controller of their own. Gemini prompts. I built the flow for generating, saving and deleting AI prompts. A rename. AppUser became User, with the table named users, because user is a reserved word in PostgreSQL. Reflections on concurrency # I tried to answer two questions: where does Atlas already run on several threads, and where would a background thread solve a real problem?
Javalin runs on Jetty, which handles each request on its own thread. So any state shared between requests (a counter, a cache, a list of open connections) has to be thread safe. It is easy to forget, because nothing breaks until two requests arrive at once. My call to Gemini is a slow network call, and it blocks the request thread while it waits. Time capsules open on a date. Something has to notice that date, and it is not a request. A new announcement could notify every user, but nobody should wait for that. My conclusion was to wait. The API was not finished, and concurrency added to an unfinished system would just be noise. I wrote down the candidates: a rate limiter for the AI calls, a scheduled job for time capsules, a thread pool for notifications and, maybe, a WebSocket.
Looking back: those four were exactly what I ended up building later in the project, and each one solved a problem I had already described here.
Challenges # The reserved word user caused a confusing database error before I understood what was wrong.
Next week # Token-based login (JWT) and a generic controller so I do not repeat the same code for every resource.
Next week #
title: Week 5 — Concurrency

content:
This week the main focus of school was integration of an api in a java project. More specifically, requesting a prompt from google gemini and extracting the data from the prompt. Because I already had a feature planned where a user could generate a prompt, containing an idea of something to write about i thought about how i could implement this in atlas.
What I worked # Javalin and the first endpoints, tested with Postman. I also made my first mapper, DTO and service (for the user). Validation for registration and login, and a getUserByEmail method in the DAO. Roles. I added a Role enum (USER, ADMIN) and a role field on the user. Visibility. I added a Visibility enum so that each page can later be private or public. Gemini. I added Jackson and made my first call to the Google Gemini API with Java’s HttpClient, and parsed the answer into a small DTO. Reflections # Integrating gemini API # When i first thought of the “prompt generator” feature, my plan was to have a list of short hard coded prompts in the database, a user could get at random. After learning how to use the gemini API in school, i decided to intergrate that in the feature. So instead of a list of prompts typed manually in the database, I could instead utilize gemini to create unique prompts every time a user asks for one.
This decision automates the feature in atlas, and in concept, would never need to be “updated” by adding new prompts once the user had seen them all, making it fully dynamic. I used the project we made together in school, and when i could sucessully extract a prompt, i made the proper mapper, DTO and DAO classes in order to show the prompt, and for the user to save a prompt they like.
Privacy # A big part of atlas is privacy. I want to ensure that a user can choose whether or not they want their created page to be private or public. Therefore i added an enum to my project called visibility. It contains “PUBLIC” and “PRIVATE”. The reason i choose an enum over a boolean, is that i originally wanted the user to between private, public or a custom setting. The idea with the custom setting was that the user could pick from a list of friends, who they wanted a page to be public with. I quickly decided though, that it was a bit out of scope, and i wanted to focus on basic privacy functionality first. If i decide to add it in the future, the enum makes it easy to add a variant of visibility, which i would not be able to, if i had chosen to use a boolean.
I also decided that the default is that everything is private when the user creates pages. Every page belongs to exactly one user, and that every query later has to be filtered on that user. It is easier to build this in from the start than to add it afterwards.
Storing Visibility before I use it. Sharing is not built yet, so the field is not used for anything. I kept it anyway, because adding a column to existing data later is more work than leaving a field unused for a while. I could also have left it out until I needed it. I chose the safer option.
Why DTOs? It would have been quicker to return the entity directly. But then the password hash would be part of the response, and clients could set any field they liked. DTOs let me decide exactly what goes in and out.
Testing Entity-Specific Behaviour # Challenges # Parsing the answer from Gemini was fiddly. The response has several nested objects, and my first attempt broke when the API added fields I did not know about. Telling Jackson to ignore unknown properties solved it.
Next week # Logging, a proper controller structure, and token-based login.
title: Week 4 — API endpoints & privacy

content:
This week I continued working on Atlas, with a focus on testing the DAO layer.
After creating the basic DAO structure, I wanted to make sure that my database operations worked as expected. I created individual test classes for my DAOs and developed a reusable TestPopulator to provide consistent test data.
I also added custom DAO methods for entities that required functionality beyond the basic CRUD operations provided by my generic DAO.
What I worked on # DAO Testing # I created a separate test class for each DAO so that I could test the functionality of each entity independently.
The tests cover operations such as creating, finding, updating, and deleting entities, as well as custom methods specific to individual DAOs.
This allowed me to test my persistence layer before moving further into the API.
Test Populator # One of the first things I needed was a reliable way of creating test data.
I created a TestPopulator class that persists several instances of each entity into the test database. I considered creating multiple smaller populators, but decided to keep one central populator because many of my entities depend on each other.
For example, a Memory can depend on a Person, Place, Chapter, or AppUser. Having all of the related entities created in one place makes it easier to construct valid test data.
After populating the database, the populator returns a SeededData record containing the persisted entities:
return new SeededData( user1, user2, user3, chapter1, chapter2, chapter3, artifact1, artifact2, artifact3, artifact4, musicType, objectType, vehicleType, fragment1, fragment2, fragment3, entityList1, memory1, memory2, memory3, person1, person2, person3, place1, place2, place3, story1, story2, story3, timeCapsule1, timeCapsule2, timeCapsule3, mention1, mention2, mention3 ); Each test class can then use this data during its setup:
@BeforeEach void setUp() { seeded = TestPopulator.populate(emf); artifactDAO = new ArtifactDAO(emf); } This gives each test a predictable starting point and avoids having to manually create the same test data in every test class.
Generic DAO & Custom Methods # As mentioned in my previous blog post, I moved the basic CRUD operations into an abstract generic DAO class.
The individual DAOs can extend this class and reuse the common functionality instead of implementing the same methods for every entity.
However, I kept the tests as separate classes rather than creating one generic DAO test.
The reason for this is that some of my entities have their own lifecycle methods and additional logic that needs to be tested when entities are created or updated. Because of this, the tests cannot always rely on the exact same behaviour.
For entities with additional functionality, I can therefore add tests specifically for that behaviour.
What I learned # Testing the Persistence Layer # This week gave me a better understanding of why testing the DAO layer is important.
Rather than only checking whether the application works when everything is connected together, I can test the database operations independently.
This makes it easier to identify where a problem occurs. If a test for a DAO fails, I can investigate the persistence logic without having to involve the API or frontend.
Creating Reusable Test Data # I also learned the importance of having a consistent way of creating test data.
Because many of my entities are connected through JPA relationships, creating test data manually inside every test would quickly become repetitive and difficult to maintain.
The TestPopulator gives me one central place where I can define the relationships between my test entities.
Testing Entity-Specific Behaviour # Another thing I learned was that not every DAO can necessarily be treated exactly the same way.
While the generic DAO handles the common CRUD functionality, individual entities can have their own business logic and lifecycle methods.
This means my tests need to cover both the shared DAO functionality and the behaviour that is specific to each entity.
Challenges & Problems # The biggest challenge this week was understanding the dependencies between my entities and creating the correct data needed to test them.
Because many entities have relationships with other entities, I could not simply create one entity in isolation.
For example, when testing an entity that requires an AppUser or another related entity, that related entity needs to exist and be persisted first.
This made the order in which the test data is created important.
It also made me realise that the structure of my test data needs to reflect the same relationships that exist in the actual application.
Next week # Next week I want to continue working towards the Atlas API.
My main focus will be on learning how to expose the functionality I have built through API endpoints and understanding how the different layers of my backend should communicate with each other.
title: Week 3 — Testing the DAO Layer

content:
This week I continued working on Atlas. I focused on the database structure, JPA relationships, and the first steps towards building the API.
I also spent time analysing the entity layer I had created previously and used it as the foundation for developing my DAOs.
What I worked on # Database & DAOs # I started working on the database layer of Atlas by looking at how my entities should interact with the database.
Based on the entity structure, I began developing DAOs (Data Access Objects) for handling database operations.
This helped me understand how the entity layer, JPA, Hibernate, and the database work together.
I also started working with relationships between entities using JPA annotations such as:
@OneToMany @OneToOne @ManyToOne These relationships allow the different parts of Atlas to be connected in the database.
Generics # In order to avoid having the same crud methods written in each DAO class, i created an abstract DAO class the extends my IDAO. Thern each DAO can extend the generic DAO in order to inherit all basic crud methods. This makes my dao classes clean as they only need their custom dao methods in the body.
i also made a generic entity “LinkableEntity”. This was a choice i took especially because of my entityList entity. Which is a feature that allows the user to make a custom list with any entity in the program that can be linked to each other. With a generic entity, the process becomes much smoother.
Annotations & Lombok # I learned more about Java annotations and how they can provide additional information to the application and influence how entities are handled by JPA and Hibernate.
I also worked with Lombok, which helped reduce the amount of boilerplate code in my entity classes.
Instead of manually writing getters, setters, constructors, and other common methods, Lombok can generate them automatically using annotations.
This made my entity classes considerably shorter and easier to maintain.
Entity Lifecycle Methods # While working on my entities, I came across two annotations that I found particularly useful: @PrePersist and @PreUpdate.
@PrePersist allows a method to run automatically before an entity is persisted to the database.
I used it to set default values for fields such as createdAt:
@PrePersist public void setDefaultDate() { if (this.createdAt == null) { this.createdAt = LocalDate.now(); } } This means I don’t have to manually set the creation date every time I create a new entity.
I also worked with @PreUpdate, which runs automatically before an existing entity is updated.
In my entities, I used it to update the updatedAt field and recalculate values such as the word count:
@PreUpdate protected void onUpdate() { updatedAt = LocalDate.now(); calculateWordCount(); } This allows certain values to be updated automatically whenever the entity changes.
What I learned # JPA Relationships # I gained a much better understanding of how entities communicate with each other through JPA relationships.
Previously, I mainly understood entities as individual classes representing database tables. Working with relationships helped me understand how these entities can instead be connected and how those connections are represented in Java.
I learned how annotations such as @OneToMany, @OneToOne, and @ManyToOne can be used to define these relationships.
For example, a user can have multiple memories, while each memory belongs to a specific user.
DAOs # I also gained a better understanding of the purpose of DAOs.
Rather than having database operations directly inside my entities or other parts of the application, the DAO provides a separate place for handling persistence-related operations.
This gave me a clearer idea of how the different layers of my backend can be separated.
Entity Lifecycle # Working with @PrePersist and @PreUpdate also helped me understand that JPA provides ways to react to different stages of an entity’s lifecycle.
This can be useful for automatically handling values such as creation dates, update dates, calculated fields, and other values that should be maintained by the application.
Challenges & Problems # One of the things I had to get used to this week was understanding how the different parts of the backend fit together.
The entity classes, JPA relationships, DAOs, Hibernate, and database are all connected, but each has a different responsibility.
Working through this helped me understand that the backend is not just about creating entities, but about creating a structure where the different layers work together.
Next week # Next week I want to continue building the Atlas API.
My main focus will be on understanding how to expose my backend functionality through API endpoints and continue developing the structure that will eventually allow the React frontend to communicate with the Java backend.
title: Week 2 — Database & Relations

content:
Project Overview # Atlas is a personal journal application designed to help users document, organize, and preserve the important parts of their lives.
The idea is to create a private, personal space where memories, people, places, stories, and meaningful objects can be collected and connected — almost like a personal Wikipedia for your own life.
The project is being developed as a full-stack application, with a Java backend API serving as the foundation and a React frontend providing the user interface.
Project Information # Developer - Andreas Jensen Education - Datamatiker — 3rd semester School - EK Year - 2026 Status - In development (backend v1 complete) Type - Full Stack Application
Goal # The goal of the project is to develop a production-oriented backend that demonstrates the principles and technologies covered throughout the semester.
The backend includes:
User authentication with JWT, and role-based access control (USER and ADMIN) Secure, user-specific data, where one user can never read another user’s pages CRUD functionality, business rules and data validation JPA and Hibernate persistence with PostgreSQL A REST API with DTOs for communication between the backend and frontend Concurrency: a scheduled job, a thread pool and thread-safe shared state Real-time notifications over a WebSocket An external API integration (Google Gemini) Automated tests of the database layer and of every endpoint A structure that can be expanded with additional functionality in the future Atlas is built around the idea of preserving your personal story.
Instead of treating memories as isolated diary entries, the application allows different parts of a person’s life to be connected.
For example, a memory about a trip to Italy could be connected to:
The people who were there The places that were visited Objects that carry meaning Related memories A larger chapter of the user’s life The user highlights a piece of text, links it to another page, and every page can then show everything that links to it. This creates a more interconnected way of documenting life rather than simply writing individual journal entries.
Core Concepts # Atlas is built around several central concepts:
Chapters and Stories Larger periods or narratives in a person’s life.
Memories Individual moments or experiences that the user wants to preserve.
People and Places The people and the locations that matter to the user’s story.
Artifacts Objects that carry personal meaning, such as albums, films, or clothing. Each user creates their own categories.
Entity Lists and Fragments Custom collections (favourite films, books, quotes) and short notes that do not need a full page.
Mentions Links from a highlighted piece of text in one page to another page. They make it possible to see which pages link to a given person, place or memory (backlinks).
Time Capsules Messages that stay sealed until a date in the future. When the date arrives, the owner is notified.
Notifications and Devlog Admins publish announcements (a changelog), and every user receives a notification. Notifications are saved in the database and pushed live to anyone who is connected.
AI journaling prompts Writing prompts generated with Google Gemini, with a limit on how many a user can request.
Architecture # The project is divided into two main parts:
Backend # The backend is developed in Java with Javalin and provides the API and business logic for Atlas.
A request passes through clear layers:
Client -> SecurityFilter (JWT, role) -> Controller -> Service -> DAO -> PostgreSQL Controllers validate the request and choose the status code. Services hold the rules, such as ownership checks. DAOs handle persistence with JPA and Hibernate. A generic DAO and a generic controller remove repeated CRUD code. DTOs and mappers keep the database entities out of the API. Dependencies are wired by hand in one place, using constructor injection. Alongside the request flow, some work runs in the background:
a scheduled thread checks time capsules and keeps WebSocket connections alive a thread pool creates devlog notifications for every user a registry of open WebSocket connections delivers notifications live Frontend # The frontend is being developed with React.
It will provide the visual interface through which users can create, view, edit, and organize their personal content.
The frontend communicates with the Java backend through the REST API and a WebSocket for live notifications.
Development # Atlas is developed as part of my 3rd-semester Datamatiker project at EK.
The project has been built incrementally: the data model and persistence layer first, then the REST API, security and tests, and finally concurrency and real-time notifications. I write a weekly log about the choices and trade-offs along the way.
The first version of the backend is complete. Features I want to build next include images on pages, search across all pages, a timeline, and friends with shared pages.
The long-term goal is to create a polished full-stack application that demonstrates both the technical concepts learned during the semester and a practical, user-focused product.
Technologies # Backend # Java Javalin (HTTP and WebSockets) JPA and Hibernate PostgreSQL JWT and BCrypt Jackson Testing # JUnit and Hamcrest REST Assured Testcontainers (a real PostgreSQL in Docker) Frontend (To be made) # React JavaScript HTML CSS Development # IntelliJ IDEA pgAdmin Docker Git / GitHub Figma (diagrams)
title: Atlas

content:
This week I started Atlas: a personal, private encyclopedia of your own life. You write pages (memories, chapters, stories, people, places, objects), highlight text in a page and link it to another page, and every page can then show what links to it.
The main goal was to establish the basic architecture of the application and create a solid foundation for the development process.
What I worked on # I set up the project from the template and removed the classes I did not need. The first student-style DAO became a UserDAO, and I created the first entities (AppUser and Chapter) and registered them in an EntityRegistry.
I also wrote my first DAO through an IDAO interface with basic CRUD, and tried it out directly in main before building anything around it.
Domain model # Below is a simplified class diagram of the domain model. My domain model was sketched by hand, which is why i dont have a good overview of that. But based on the domain model, i made this class diagram that represent the entire project truly.
Reflections # Why start with entities and a DAO? Everything else in the project depends on the data model. If a relationship is wrong here, it is wrong in the API, the tests and the frontend too. Starting at the bottom felt slow, but I think it was cheaper than fixing the structure later.
How I implemented it. # Created the initial project structure with the use of a domain model. Started designing the database. I did so by designing an ER diagram, to have a better visual understanding of the system architecture Worked with JPA and Hibernate Created the first entities and added relations between the classes Noticeable changes # Changed the datatype from “int” to “Integer” on my entities id attribute, in order for the “equals” and “hash” methods to be compatible with the id. Next week # Next week we will be introduced to data intergration and how to implement the use of api’s in java. I will also be working on finishing setting up my DAO classes and create test to make sure they correctly can communicate wit the database.
Create all the entities, connect them with JPA relationships, and start on a generic DAO so I do not write the same CRUD code over and over.
title: Week 1 — Getting Started

content:
I’m Andreas — a full-stack developer building things with Java, React, and PostgreSQL.
Write a paragraph or two here about yourself, your background, and what you’re currently working on or interested in.
title: About
